AFAQ Space 🚀

An award-winning crew of space enthusiasts, game designers and engineers, spanning full-stack, mobile, AI, robotics and game. 

We build fast, and we’re here to win.
summary:
What if a student could design a real space mission, fly it, and find out exactly why it worked or failed?

Mission Horizon is a mission-design game for students aged 12 and up. You set the science objective, then choose the orbit, a real NASA spacecraft, the launch day, the rocket and the instruments, while six gauges stay in balance: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. One red gauge and the mission does not launch.

Then you fly it by hand through five stages: launch, transfer, cruise, orbit insertion and science. A mission report explains every result with the number that decided it and names the trade-off that made the difference.

The physics is real, and it is checked. Asked for the cheapest 2020 departure to Mars, our engine answers 19 July 2020, the day the UAE's Hope probe launched. 172 automated checks against NASA and JPL figures, including a GMAT lunar trajectory, run live inside the game.

Eight more mission scenarios, from a Moon lander to a Jupiter orbiter, are graded the way NASA grades real concepts: by the four mission segments and JPL's Concept Maturity Levels. Up to four students play as one mission team, each with a role and private information.

Played on hackathon day by organisers, rival teams and visitors. Fully bilingual in Arabic and English, on phones, tablets, computers and VR headsets. Challenge 13 asks for trade-offs that stop being abstract. Here, you have to close a real design and then fly it.
details:
Students are told that every space mission is a compromise. They almost never get to make that compromise themselves.

Mission Horizon hands them the whole mission. Add an instrument and the power gauge can turn red. Choose a bigger antenna and the mass climbs. Pick a cheaper rocket and the orbit may be out of reach. Then they fly what they designed, and the report shows which decision settled the outcome, with its number.

Start here: the two-minute judge demo. Open afaq.afai.om/game/mission?demo=1 and the game flies a complete Mars mission by itself, so you see all eight steps before you play: (1) the mission briefing, (2) the hangar, where the spacecraft is designed, (3) launch, (4) the transfer burn, (5) the cruise and its space-weather decisions, (6) Mars orbit insertion, (7) science operations, and (8) the mission report that explains every result. You can stop the demo and take the controls at any step. Everything described below is in the live game today.

The mission loop: design, fly, understand

  • Design under real constraints. Pick a real NASA spacecraft in 3D and a launch day on a porkchop plot, then swap the bus, power source, engine, antenna, instruments and rocket. Six live gauges (mass, power, budget, data, communications and time) react to every change. A red gauge blocks the launch and says what would fix it, and the rocket is checked against the craft's mass and the chosen orbit.
  • Fly the mission by hand. Five stages: steer the rocket to orbit, time the transfer burn, decide under real space-weather events during the cruise, fire the orbit-insertion burn, then wait out the true light-time delay and point the instruments.
  • Understand every outcome. The mission report lists each decision, gives each stage's result with its deciding number, names the trade-off that decided the mission, and compares the flight with real missions such as Hope, MAVEN and MRO.
  • Three levels of help. Trainee, Engineer and Flight Director change how much guidance the player gets. The physics never changes.

More than ten missions, graded the NASA way

  • Mission scenarios. Beyond the Mars orbiter: Earth observation, a Moon orbiter, a Moon lander, a Jupiter orbiter, a telescope at Sun-Earth L2, a Mars rover landing, an asteroid sample return, planetary defence (redo NASA's DART impact) and a sandbox, with simple and advanced difficulty and random events.
  • Graded the NASA way. Each scenario report splits the mission into NASA's four segments (launch, space, ground, user) and scores it with JPL's Concept Maturity Level checklist, CML 1 to 4, including the CML 4 margins of 35% mass and power and a 3 dB link margin. A live CML strip on the design screen shows which Goddard Mission Design Lab study the design has reached and what is missing for the next level.

Play as a mission team, or compete

  • Team play for up to four. Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Comms and Resources. Each role maps to seats of NASA Goddard's Mission Design Lab, holds private information, and votes on proposals whose consequences are computed first. The team makes the GO / NO-GO call together, on one shared device or online.
  • The Arena. A daily challenge with the same seed for everyone, 72-hour duels, live race rooms, and leaderboards (global, weekly, crew and class). Any design can be shared as a short code.

Step inside: 3D, AR, VR and 360° video

  • 3D. 116 NASA 3D models, each one spinnable. Fifteen spacecraft, from Voyager 1 to JWST, open up with numbered hotspots, an x-ray view, an exploded view and a cutaway.
  • AR. Place a spacecraft in your room through the camera: AR Quick Look on iPhone and iPad, and on the web. The Mars rovers and the Ingenuity helicopter appear at life size.
  • VR. Stand beside your spacecraft above a planet in WebXR, on Meta Quest, in a Cardboard viewer, or with the phone as a moving window. A guided planet tour goes from the Sun to Saturn with captions in Arabic and English.
  • 360° video. 30 official NASA and ESA 360-degree films, such as Mission Control on Perseverance's landing day, Cassini's Grand Finale and the ISS modules. They also appear inside Academy lessons.

Live NASA data: "Space now"

One screen shows what is happening in space this minute. Every tile names its source and the age of its data, and adds one sentence on what it means for a mission designer.

  • Deep Space Network: which antenna is talking to which spacecraft (NASA DSN Now).
  • Space weather: solar flares, storms, the Kp index and the solar wind (NASA DONKI and NOAA SWPC).
  • Asteroids: close approaches and the Sentry impact-risk table (JPL CNEOS).
  • Earth events: fires, storms and volcanoes (NASA EONET), and Earth images from EPIC.
  • ISS and far probes: the station's position every five seconds, and where the distant probes are now (JPL Horizons), with the light-time to each.

Learn as you play

An Academy of 8 courses and 56 lessons with quizzes, a 12-question exam and a verifiable certificate for each course, and a unit called "The NASA way" built on this challenge's own resources. Classroom mode gives the teacher a join code, a dashboard, a CSV export and a before/after Mission Readiness Check.

How it works

  • One physics engine: pure TypeScript with a Lambert solver, JPL planet positions, porkchop plots, patched conics and gravity assists, the rocket equation with staging, solar and RTG power, a term-by-term link budget, Earth orbits with J2 and drag, lunar transfers, Lagrange points, Mars entry and landing, sample return and asteroid deflection. Every formula cites its source in the code.
  • No shortcuts in the game layer: budgets, flight results, the risk model and the score all read the same engine output.
  • Honest numbers: every number on screen is labelled as official (published by an agency), engine (computed and validated) or game rule (a design choice such as a margin), and touching it shows the source.

Validated against NASA

172 automated science checks against NASA and JPL figures run live on the in-game Science screen. Highlights:

  • Hope's launch day: asked for the cheapest 2020 Earth-to-Mars departure, the engine answers 19 July 2020, the day the UAE's Hope probe launched.
  • Juno at Jupiter: orbit-insertion burn 526 m/s (impulsive) vs 542 m/s published by NASA JPL.
  • Mars 2026 window: launch energy 9.143 vs 9.144 km²/s² (NASA/TM-2010-216764).
  • DART: impact speed 6.15 vs 6.1 km/s (Final DART Technical Report).
  • Voyager 2: Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus flyby distances rebuilt from launch and encounter dates alone.
  • GMAT and Mission Viz: the engine checked against a GMAT Earth-to-Moon trajectory and the planetary elements published in NASA Mission Viz, both Challenge 13 resources.

Built on the Challenge 13 NASA resources

  • Design and Develop Science Missions (NASA): the four mission segments structure the scenario report.
  • Concept Maturity Levels (JPL): the CML ladder and CML 4 checklist grade every scenario design.
  • Mission Design Lab (NASA Goddard): its study types and 16 engineering disciplines shape the CML strip and the team roles.
  • GMAT and NASA Mission Viz: reference trajectories and orbital elements for engine validation.
  • CubeSat 101 (NASA CSLI): the 6U bus data and an Academy lesson on sizes, schedules and licensing.
  • Webb "Build It Yourself": we keep its science-first loop and add what it leaves out: budget, mass, power, communications, risk and team play.
  • Space Apps 2023 VR challenge: the WebXR tour for headsets.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Learning by doing: students try a whole mission instead of reading about one, and every failure names its cause, its number and its lesson.
  • Access: fully bilingual (Arabic and English), runs on ordinary phones and tablets, and the solo game works offline.
  • Classrooms: one device for a team of four, or a whole class with a shared mission and a before/after readiness check.
  • First playtest: on hackathon day the game was played by four event organisers, members of competing teams and visitors from outside the event, as well as our own team. They stayed engaged through the mission and the feedback was strongly positive.
  • Next steps: playtests in schools in Oman, starting in Ibra.

Creativity

Instead of filling in a form, the player flies every stage of the mission. Roles hold private information that forces real negotiation, and scenario designs are graded with the same maturity checklist NASA and JPL use for real mission concepts. NASA's own Webb game, listed in the challenge resources, links goals to instruments but has no budget, mass, power or team play; Mission Horizon adds all of them, with real physics.

Design considerations

  • Accuracy first: no number appears in the game without a published source or a validated computation.
  • Accessibility: right-to-left Arabic layout built in, screen-reader labels, keyboard focus, a reduced-motion setting, spoken mission-control callouts, and layouts from phone to desktop.
  • Privacy: accounts are optional; the game collects no personal data to play.

Tools and technologies

  • App: TypeScript, Expo SDK 57, React Native, Expo Router, React Native Reanimated, react-native-svg.
  • 3D and XR: three.js, WebXR, model-viewer and Apple AR Quick Look.
  • Backend: self-hosted Supabase (optional accounts, classes and online team play), Docker and nginx.
  • Platforms: web, iPhone and iPad, Android and Meta Quest.
